sentences.text: Mai told her parents that night.
Her father was silent for a long moment.
Then he said, "Ông Lâm is the most respected lantern maker in Hoi An.
If he has chosen you, this is — this is a very serious honor, Mai.
Very serious.
I do not know if I would be brave enough to do it if he had chosen me.
It is a lot to ask of a ten-year-old." Her mother said, "You can say no if you are not ready.
It is not — you do not have to say yes just because he asked.
That is what being brave means.
Being brave enough to say no." Her father added, "But also being brave enough to say yes."
Mai lay in bed for hours that night.
She thought about what would happen if she dropped the string.
If the wind took the lantern before she was ready.
If the lantern caught fire.
If she cried in front of everyone.
She thought about all the ways it could go wrong.
Then she thought about the small blue moon lantern she did not even remember pointing at.
She thought about how Ông Lâm had waited three years.
She thought about how he had decided that a small girl who noticed things was the right one.
If she said no, that would mean he was wrong.
But he did not seem wrong.
He had seemed very sure.
On Friday she walked to Ông Lâm's shop.
She walked slowly.
She was still afraid.
When she got to the door, she stopped for a moment.
Then she went in.
Ông Lâm was there.
He looked up.
He waited.
Mai said, "I will do it, Ông Lâm." Ông Lâm nodded once.
He said, "Good.
Come.
We start now."
He took out a long thin bamboo string, three meters long, with a small wooden handle on one end.
He said, "This is the practice string.
It is the same length as the string on the fish lantern.
Every day for three weeks, we will practice with it.
First we practice holding.
Then we practice standing.
Then we practice with wind.
Then we practice with everything.
If in the last week you decide you cannot do it, that is fine.
You can still say no.
But we will practice as if you are going to say yes."
The first thing he taught her was how to stand.
This was harder than she had expected.
She had to hold the string straight up above her head, one hand on the handle at the bottom, the other hand about a meter up the string for control.
She had to stand with her feet apart and her back straight.
She had to breathe slowly.
She had to not lock her knees.
She had to feel the string as if it was — Ông Lâm said this many times — as if it was a small living thing.
"Do not fight it," he said.
"The string is not against you.
The lantern is not against you.
The wind is not against you.
All of it is together.
You are part of it.
If you fight, you tense up, and you drop the string.
If you relax, and you stay with it, you will hold it as long as it needs to be held."
For the first week Mai practiced only standing.
Every afternoon she went to Ông Lâm's small courtyard.
She stood with the empty practice string.
Ông Lâm watched her.
He corrected small things — her elbows, her breathing, the way her feet were set.
He was patient.
He never seemed disappointed.
On the fourth day she was so tired her arms shook and she had to lower the string.
She thought Ông Lâm would be upset.
He was not.
He said, "Yes.
That is what tired feels like.
Now you know.
Rest.
In a minute, we do it again."
In the second week they added the wind.
Ông Lâm had a small paper kite the size of her hand, which he tied to the top of the practice string.
It caught the wind and pulled the string sideways.
Mai had to hold on.
She had to lean into the pull.
She had to not fight it — she had to move with it.
This was much harder.
The kite pulled her off balance.
Twice she fell over.
Ông Lâm helped her up.
He did not laugh.
He said, "Good.
Now you have fallen.
Everyone falls the first time.
Now you know what falling feels like."
In the third week Ông Lâm brought her into the workshop.
The fish lantern was almost finished.
The bamboo frame was already built — it took up the whole floor.
He was covering it now with layers of thin painted silk.
Mai watched him work.
She was allowed to help with small things — holding one edge of the silk while he glued, passing him tools when he asked.
She was not allowed to touch the frame with unclean hands.
She was not allowed to lean over it.
"This lantern," Ông Lâm said, gluing a fin, "took me two months to make.
The bamboo was cut in July.
The silk was dyed in August.
Now, in September, we finish it.
On the night of the festival, we light it.
It will fly for maybe twenty minutes.
Then the paper will burn away and the lantern will fall gently into the river and float downstream and eventually sink.
That is the whole life of this lantern.
Two months to make.
Twenty minutes to fly.
Then gone." He looked up at Mai.
"That is why the person who holds the string has to be a person who understands that this is not — this is not about keeping.
It is about letting go.
The whole point is the letting go."
